author: Alexander Hamilton
title: Report on Manufactures (excerpt)
locator: The Papers of Alexander Hamilton 10:338–340; The Founders’ Constitution, vol. 3, art. I §8 cl. 8, doc. 9
note: Hamilton proposed public funds to encourage inventions, bring in skilled manufacturers, and overcome limits of private capital. This supports interpreting manufacturing capacity as a political project.
caution: This is an excerpt, not the complete report; it proves advocacy, not implementation or policy success.
verification: Page opened and relevant text verified

author: Harriet Jane Hanson Robinson
title: Loom and Spindle; or, Life among the Early Mill Girls
locator: Chapter V, Characteristics (Continued), account of October 1836 strike
note: A former Lowell worker recalled women collectively leaving the mills when pay was threatened. Factory employment offered wages but also created conflicts over control of those wages.
caution: Retrospective memoir published decades after the event; an individual perspective, not a representative wage survey.
verification: Page opened and relevant text verified

author: Andrew Carnegie
title: The Gospel of Wealth
locator: Opening discussion of wealth concentration and industrial production
note: Carnegie defended concentrated wealth and assigned wealthy owners a philanthropic role. Read this as an industrialist’s justification of inequality, not evidence that workers shared equally in prosperity.
caution: Original essay reprinted by Carnegie Corporation; author has a direct stake in the system he defends.
verification: Official institutional PDF indexed and text verified

author: United States Congress
title: Sherman Anti-Trust Act
locator: Transcript, §§1–2; National Archives, RG 11
note: The law prohibited certain restraints of interstate trade and monopolization. Its existence reveals political conflict over corporate concentration.
caution: Legislation establishes a rule and intent, not evidence of immediate effective enforcement.
verification: Page opened and relevant text verified

author: Henry Ford with Samuel Crowther
title: My Life and Work
locator: Chapter V, Getting into Production; flywheel-magneto assembly experiment
note: Ford described dividing assembly into operations and moving work between workers, beginning experiments in 1913. The account illustrates redesign of production and work.
caution: Owner-authored retrospective account. Do not credit Ford with inventing all assembly-line methods; distinguish experiments in components from moving chassis assembly.
verification: Page opened and relevant text verified

author: United States Congress
title: National Industrial Recovery Act
locator: Transcript, Title I, §1 and §7
note: The Act linked recovery, industrial organization, consumption, and labor standards. It shows that the Depression prompted experiments in governing production.
caution: Intent is not an estimate of economic effect. Major code provisions were struck down in 1935.
verification: Page opened and relevant text verified

author: United States Congress
title: National Labor Relations Act (Wagner Act)
locator: Original enrolled-act scan and introductory account; RG 11
note: The 1935 Act protected collective organization and bargaining and established the NLRB. It provides a concrete institutional mechanism linking factory work and bargaining power.
caution: IMPORTANT: the page’s HTML transcript is explicitly the Act AS AMENDED SINCE 1935. Do not present its entire current wording as the original 1935 text.
verification: National Archives page indexed and text verified

author: Franklin D. Roosevelt
title: Executive Order 8802: Prohibition of Discrimination in the Defense Industry
locator: Transcript, preamble and numbered provisions 1–3; RG 11
note: The order prohibited racial and other specified discrimination in defense employment and created a fair-employment committee. It documents that wartime job growth coexisted with exclusion.
caution: An order is evidence of a policy response, not proof that discrimination ended.
verification: National Archives page indexed and full transcript verified

author: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
title: Industrial Production and Capacity Utilization, G.17
locator: Opening release paragraph and Summary table
note: The release reported manufacturing’s sharp March–April fall and partial May rebound as factories resumed operations. Rebound growth did not mean that the pre-pandemic level had been restored.
caution: Contemporaneous release vintage; its 2012=100 index and preliminary values must not be spliced into a current-vintage 2017=100 series.
verification: Page opened and relevant text verified

author: United States Congress
title: CHIPS and Science Act, Public Law 117–167
note: The statute established semiconductor support and an advanced manufacturing investment credit. It connects industrial policy to domestic capacity and supply-chain concerns.
caution: A funding authorization or appropriation is not completed factory output, jobs created, or proof of program success.
verification: Page opened and relevant text verified

author: National Park Service, Lowell National Historical Park
title: The Mill Girls of Lowell
locator: Introduction; Choices and Changes; A New Way to Live and Work
note: Lowell recruited young women into cotton factories. Cash wages could offer independence, while long hours and corporate control constrained it.
caution: Modern public-history interpretation, not an original nineteenth-century document.
verification: Official page indexed and relevant text verified

author: National Park Service, Lowell National Historical Park
title: Southern Ties & Northern Gospels
locator: Southern Ties: Lowell Manufacturing Company
note: Northern textile businesses depended on cotton produced by enslaved labor; some also sold cloth to enslavers. Northern factory growth was entangled with Southern slavery.
caution: Modern historical account. Do not label the whole page primary merely because it contains historical images.
verification: Official page indexed and relevant text verified

author: Library of Congress
title: Ford Implements the Moving Assembly Line
locator: Opening narrative, October 1913 Highland Park
note: Ford’s moving assembly line at Highland Park expanded automobile production and reduced assembly time. It drew on techniques used in other industries.
caution: Institutional retrospective account. Factory-specific efficiency is not a national manufacturing productivity estimate.
verification: Official page indexed and relevant text verified

author: Katelynn Harris, U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics
title: Forty years of falling manufacturing employment
locator: Steady, cyclical growth, 1939–79; Declines after 1979
note: Manufacturing payroll jobs peaked at about 19.6 million in June 1979. Later cyclical recoveries did not restore that employment peak.
caution: Article is secondary analysis; its underlying CES series is primary statistical data. Monthly peak differs from annual mean. Does not itself identify the causes of job losses.
verification: Page opened and relevant text verified

author: Michael Corbett, Federal Reserve History
title: Oil Shock of 1973–74
locator: Opening historical account
note: The 1973 embargo and oil-price shock complicated an economy already facing industrial price pressures. This is context for the decade’s disruptions.
caution: Context does not identify how much of manufacturing employment change oil alone caused.
verification: Page opened and relevant text verified

author: David H. Autor, David Dorn, and Gordon H. Hanson
title: The China Syndrome: Local Labor Market Effects of Import Competition in the United States
locator: American Economic Review 103(6):2121–2168; linked NBER working paper 18054 (May 2012), DOI 10.3386/w18054
note: The authors connect greater import exposure during 1990–2007 to worse labor-market outcomes in exposed U.S. localities. Trade shocks are one documented cause rather than a complete explanation of all manufacturing decline.
caution: Academic analysis is secondary for this history project, even though it reports original empirical research. Distinguish 2012 working paper from 2013 journal article.
verification: NBER metadata and abstract indexed and verified

author: Daron Acemoglu and Pascual Restrepo
title: Robots and Jobs: Evidence from US Labor Markets
locator: Journal of Political Economy 128(6):2188–2244; abstract and introduction; DOI 10.1086/705716
note: The study estimates negative employment and wage effects from greater industrial-robot exposure across U.S. commuting zones. Technological change can affect workers differently from aggregate output.
caution: Study concerns industrial robots and historical local labor markets; do not generalize it to all technology, all periods, or every lost factory job.
verification: Page opened and relevant text verified

author: Susan N. Houseman
title: Understanding the Decline of U.S. Manufacturing Employment
locator: Upjohn Institute Working Paper 18–287; January, revised June 2018; DOI 10.17848/wp18-287
note: Houseman cautions that computer-sector quality adjustment and aggregation shape measured output and productivity. Output-per-worker growth alone cannot establish automation as the cause of job losses.
caution: This challenges a simple interpretation of aggregate statistics; it does not establish that robots never displace workers.
verification: Page opened and relevant text verified

author: David Autor, David Dorn, and Gordon H. Hanson
title: On the Persistence of the China Shock
locator: NBER Working Paper 29401, October 2021; DOI 10.3386/w29401; abstract
note: The authors find adverse employment and income effects in more exposed local labor markets persisting to 2019. Aggregate recovery can coexist with geographically concentrated losses.
caution: Evidence concerns differential exposure and specified outcomes through 2019; not a forecast or a claim that every region declined.
verification: NBER metadata and abstract indexed and verified; direct open returned 403
